question: When can an agency award a contract without full and open competition because only one source can do the work?
key_facts: only one responsible source
answer: An agency may award without full and open competition when the supplies or services required are available from only one responsible source (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, from only one or a limited number of responsible sources) and no other type of supplies or services will satisfy the agency’s requirements [1][3]. Examples and applications include: an unsolicited research proposal demonstrating a unique, innovative concept or unique capability not otherwise available to the Government; and follow-on contracts for continued development/production of a major system or highly specialized equipment (or, for DoD/NASA/Coast Guard, highly specialized services) when award to another source would cause substantial duplication of cost or unacceptable delays [1]. When used, this authority: must be supported by the written justifications and approvals in 6.303 and 6.304; the notices required by 5.201 must have been published and any bids/proposals/capability statements considered; and brand-name descriptions peculiar to one manufacturer do not provide full and open competition and require justification and approval under 6.303/6.304 (with the justification posted with the solicitation) [4][8]. Additional policy constraints include that the authority is subject to the statutory authorities in 6.302, contracting officers must solicit offers from as many potential sources as practicable, and the authority must not be used to excuse lack of advance planning or funding concerns [2][3][8].

question: How long can a contract awarded under unusual and compelling urgency last?
key_facts: may not exceed one year including options, unless head of agency determines exceptional circumstances
answer: The total period of performance may not exceed the time necessary to (A) meet the unusual and compelling requirements and (B) for the agency to enter into another contract using competitive procedures, and the period “may not exceed one year, including all options,” unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply (that determination must be documented in the contract file). Any subsequent modification that causes the cumulative period using this authority to exceed one year requires a separate determination approved at the same delegation level. These requirements apply to any contract in an amount greater than the simplified acquisition threshold. [1]

question: Who has to approve a justification for other than full and open competition, and how does it depend on dollar value?
key_facts: tiered approval up to the senior procurement executive
answer:
Approval levels are set by FAR 6.304 as follows (include the estimated dollar value of all options when determining approval level) [1][1(d)]:
- For a proposed contract not exceeding $900,000: the contracting officer’s certification required by 6.303-2(b)(12) will serve as approval (unless agency procedures set a higher approving level) [1].
- For a proposed contract over $900,000 but not exceeding $20 million: approval by the advocate for competition for the procuring activity designated pursuant to 6.501, or an official described in paragraph (a)(3) or (4) of 6.304; this authority is not delegable [1].
- For a proposed contract over $20 million but not exceeding $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, not exceeding $150 million): approval by the head of the procuring activity, or a designee who (i) if a member of the armed forces, is a general or flag officer; or (ii) if a civilian, is serving in a position in a grade above GS-15 (or comparable); see 6.304(a)(3) [1].
- For a proposed contract over $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, over $150 million): approval by the senior procurement executive of the agency designated pursuant to 41 U.S.C. 1702(c); this authority is not delegable except as noted for the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment for DoD [1].
Other points: (1) Any justification for a contract awarded under 6.302-7, regardless of dollar amount, is considered approved when the determination required by 6.302-7(c)(1) is made [1(b)]. (2) Class justifications are approved in writing in accordance with agency procedures and the approval level is determined by the estimated total value of the class [1(c)]. (3) For Federal Supply Schedule orders or BPAs, parallel approval thresholds apply in FAR 8.405-6(d) (ordering-activity CO cert for orders/BPAs not exceeding $900,000; advocate for competition for >$900,000 to $20M; head of procuring activity for >$20M to $90M (or DoD/NASA/Coast Guard to $150M); senior procurement executive for >$90M (or >$150M for those agencies)) [6].

question: What must a justification for other than full and open competition contain?
key_facts: list of required contents incl. description of supplies/services, authority cited
answer: The justification must contain sufficient facts and rationale to justify the specific authority cited [2(a)]. As a minimum (except sole-source 8(a) over $30 million), it must include: (1) identification of the agency and contracting activity and that the document is a “Justification for other than full and open competition”; (2) nature/description of the action; (3) description of supplies/services required (including estimated value); (4) identification of the statutory authority permitting other than full and open competition; (5) demonstration that the proposed contractor’s unique qualifications or the nature of the acquisition requires use of the authority; (6) description of efforts to solicit offers from as many sources as practicable and whether notice was or will be publicized or which exception under 5.202 applies; (7) contracting officer determination that anticipated cost to the Government will be fair and reasonable; (8) description of market research conducted and results or statement why market research was not conducted; (9) any other supporting facts (including items (i)–(iii) listed in 6.303-2(b)(9)); (10) listing of sources, if any, that expressed written interest; (11) statement of actions the agency may take to remove or overcome barriers to competition before subsequent acquisitions; and (12) contracting officer certification that the justification is accurate and complete to the best of the contracting officer’s knowledge and belief [2(b)(1)–(12)]. The justification must also include evidence that supporting data provided by technical or requirements personnel have been certified as complete and accurate by those personnel [2(c)]. For sole-source 8(a) contracts over $30 million, the justification must, at minimum, include: (1) a description of the agency’s needs covered by the contract; (2) specification of the statutory provision providing the exception (see 19.805-1); (3) a determination that sole-source is in the agency’s best interest; (4) a determination that anticipated cost will be fair and reasonable; and (5) such other matters as the head of the agency specifies [6(d)(1)–(5)].

question: What is the micro-purchase threshold?
key_facts: $15,000 (with exceptions)
answer: The micro-purchase threshold means $15,000, except: (1) for construction subject to 40 U.S.C. chapter 31, subchapter IV, Wage Rate Requirements (Construction), it is $2,000; (2) for services subject to 41 U.S.C. chapter 67, Service Contract Labor Standards, it is $2,500; (3) for supplies or services the head of the agency determines are to support a contingency operation, certain disaster or defense responses, the threshold is $25,000 for contracts/purchases inside the United States and $40,000 for contracts/purchases outside the United States (see 13.201(g)(1)); and (4) for acquisitions from institutions of higher education or certain nonprofit research entities it is $15,000 or a higher threshold as determined by the head of the agency consistent with specified audit/risk criteria [see text].

question: What is the simplified acquisition threshold?
key_facts: $350,000 (with exceptions)
answer: The simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000, except for— (1) acquisitions to support a contingency operation; to facilitate defense against or recovery from cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack; to facilitate provision of international disaster assistance; or to support response to an emergency or major disaster, in which case it means— (i) $1 million for any contract to be awarded and performed, or purchase to be made, inside the United States; and (ii) $2 million for any contract to be awarded and performed, or purchase to be made, outside the United States; and (2) acquisitions to support a humanitarian or peacekeeping operation, in which case it means $650,000 for any contract to be awarded and performed, or purchase to be made, outside the United States.

question: How many days before issuing a solicitation must a notice of proposed contract action be published?
key_facts: at least 15 days
answer: A notice must be published at least 15 days before issuance of a solicitation. Exceptions: for acquisitions of commercial products or commercial services the contracting officer may establish a shorter period for issuance of the solicitation or use the combined synopsis and solicitation procedure; other timing rules in 5.203 (e.g., mandatory 30- and 45-day response times for certain actions) also apply as specified in 5.203 [see 5.203(a)].

question: When is a contracting officer not required to publish a synopsis of a proposed contract action?
key_facts: list of exceptions
answer: A contracting officer need not publish the synopsis when one of the exceptions in FAR 5.202 applies. Those exceptions include when the contracting officer determines that—(1) the synopsis cannot be worded to preclude disclosure that would compromise national security; (2) the proposed contract action is made under the conditions described in 6.302-2 (or, for simplified acquisitions, unusual and compelling urgency precludes competition to the maximum extent practicable) and the Government would be seriously injured if the agency complies with the time periods specified in 5.203; (3) the action is required by a foreign government’s written direction or by terms of an international agreement; (4) the action is expressly authorized or required by statute to be made through another Government agency or a specific source; (5) the action is for utility services (other than telecommunications) and only one source is available; (6) the action is an order placed under subpart 16.5; (7) the action results from acceptance under the Small Business Innovation Development Act of 1982; (8) the action results from acceptance of an unsolicited research proposal meeting the criteria in 5.202(a)(8); (9) the action is for perishable subsistence supplies where advance notice is not appropriate or reasonable; or (10) the action is made under conditions described in 6.302-3, 6.302-5 (with regard to brand name commercial products for authorized resale), or 6.302-7 and advance notice is not appropriate or reasonable. In addition, under emergency acquisition flexibilities, a contracting officer need not submit a synopsis when there is an unusual and compelling urgency and the Government would be seriously injured if the agency complied with the notice time periods (see 5.202(a)(2)). [2][1]

question: When may a time-and-materials contract be used?
key_facts: only when not possible to estimate extent/duration or costs with confidence; D&F required
answer: A time-and-materials contract may be used only when "it is not possible at the time of placing the contract to estimate accurately the extent or duration of the work or to anticipate costs with any reasonable degree of confidence." [1] In addition, before using a T&M contract the contracting officer must prepare a determination and findings that no other contract type is suitable (signed prior to execution of the base period or any option periods), and if the base period plus any option periods exceeds three years the head of the contracting activity must approve the determination and findings; the contract or order must include a ceiling price that the contractor exceeds at its own risk. [2][1]

question: When is a firm-fixed-price contract appropriate?
key_facts: reasonably definite specifications, fair and reasonable price can be established
answer: A firm-fixed-price contract is appropriate when the contracting officer can establish fair and reasonable prices at the outset — for example, when it is used to acquire commercial products or commercial services, or other supplies or services based on reasonably definite functional or detailed specifications — and one or more of these conditions exists: (a) there is adequate price competition; (b) there are reasonable price comparisons with prior purchases of the same or similar items made on a competitive basis or supported by valid certified cost or pricing data; (c) available cost or pricing information permits realistic estimates of probable costs of performance; or (d) performance uncertainties can be identified and reasonable estimates of their cost impact can be made and the contractor is willing to accept a firm fixed price representing assumption of the risks involved. A firm-fixed-price contract provides a price not subject to adjustment based on the contractor’s cost experience and places maximum risk and full responsibility for costs and resulting profit or loss on the contractor. [16.202-1; 16.202-2(a)–(d)][6][3]

question: When must the Certificate of Independent Price Determination be included in a solicitation?
key_facts: firm-fixed-price or FPEPA contracts, with exceptions
answer: The contracting officer must insert the provision at 52.203-2 (Certificate of Independent Price Determination) in solicitations when a firm-fixed-price contract or fixed-price contract with economic price adjustment is contemplated, unless—(a) the acquisition is to be made under the simplified acquisition procedures in part 13; (b) [Reserved]; (c) the solicitation is a request for technical proposals under two-step sealed bidding procedures; or (d) the solicitation is for utility services for which rates are set by law or regulation [1]. (The provision text is prescribed in 3.103-1 and appears at 52.203-2) [2].

question: When must a contracting officer set aside an acquisition for small businesses?
key_facts: rule of two: reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses at fair market prices
answer: The contracting officer shall set aside an individual acquisition or class of acquisitions for competition among small businesses when either (1) “it is determined to be in the interest of maintaining or mobilizing the Nation’s full productive capacity, war or national defense programs,” or (2) “assuring that a fair proportion of Government contracts in each industry is placed with small business concerns,” and the circumstances described in 19.502-2 or 19.502-3(a) exist. The requirement in paragraph (a) does not apply to purchases at or below the micro-purchase threshold or purchases from required sources under part 8 [19.502-1(a)–(b)] [1]. For acquisitions above the micro-purchase threshold but not over the simplified acquisition threshold, the CO shall set aside the acquisition for small business unless the CO determines there is not a reasonable expectation of obtaining offers from two or more responsible small business concerns that are competitive in terms of fair market prices, quality, and delivery; if only one acceptable small business offer is received the CO should make award to that firm; if no acceptable offers are received the set-aside shall be withdrawn and the requirement resolicited unrestricted [19.502-2(a)] [4]. For acquisitions over the simplified acquisition threshold, the CO shall set aside when there is a reasonable expectation that (1) offers will be obtained from at least two responsible small business concerns and (2) award will be made at fair market prices [19.502-2(b)] [4]. When a total set-aside is not appropriate, the CO shall set aside a portion or portions (except construction) for exclusive small business participation if the conditions in 19.502-3(a) are met (e.g., requirement can be divided into distinct portions; two or more responsible small businesses are reasonably expected to submit competitive offers; acquisition is not subject to simplified acquisition procedures; applicable program eligibility requirements apply) and the solicitation will result in a contract other than a multiple-award contract [19.502-3(a)–(c)] [5].

question: What are the limitations on subcontracting for a small business set-aside?
key_facts: percentage limits on amounts paid to non-similarly-situated subcontractors
answer: For small-business set-asides, the contractor must meet percentage limits on work performed by subcontractors that are not “similarly situated” entities: (i) Services (except construction): the concern may not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities. (ii) Supplies/products (other than procurements from a nonmanufacturer): the concern may not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance, excluding the cost of materials, to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities. (iii) General construction: the concern may not pay more than 85 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance, excluding the cost of materials, to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities. (iv) Construction by special trade contractors: the concern may not pay more than 75 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance, excluding the cost of materials, to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities. Any work that a similarly situated entity further subcontracts counts toward the applicable subcontracting percentage. The clause’s definition of “similarly situated entity” and the rule that an independent contractor is a subcontractor apply. Contractors must comply with these limitations by the end of the base term (and each option period thereafter) or by the end of the performance period for each order, at the contracting officer’s discretion. These rules apply as provided for small-business set-asides (including applicability above the simplified acquisition threshold and certain awards regardless of dollar value).

question: When does a contracting officer have to obtain certified cost or pricing data?
key_facts: above the $2,000,000 threshold unless an exception in 15.403-1(b) applies
answer:
A contracting officer must obtain certified cost or pricing data when—
- None of the exceptions in 15.403-1(b) applies and the action exceeds the applicable threshold: $950,000 for prime contracts awarded before July 1, 2018, and $2.5 million for prime contracts awarded on or after July 1, 2018; thresholds adjusted for inflation per 1.109 apply as described in the clause [15.403-4(a)]. [5][8]
- Specifically, certified cost or pricing data are required before: (i) award of any negotiated contract (except undefinitized actions), (ii) award of a subcontract at any tier if the contractor and each higher-tier subcontractor were required to furnish certified cost or pricing data, and (iii) modification of any sealed bid or negotiated contract or any covered subcontract when the pricing action is expected to exceed the threshold (including certain negotiated final pricing actions) [15.403-4(a)(1)(i)–(iii)]. [5]
- When certified cost or pricing data are required, the contracting officer shall require submission of the certified data and a Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data and include the executed certificate in the contract file [15.403-4(b); 15.406-2(a)]. [2][4]
Conditions and exceptions: certified cost or pricing data shall not be obtained for acquisitions at or below the simplified acquisition threshold, and the contracting officer must not require certified data when any exception in 15.403-1(b) applies (e.g., adequate price competition, prices set by law or regulation, commercial items, waivers) [15.403-1(a)–(b)–(c)]. The head of the contracting activity (HCA) may authorize obtaining certified data for actions below the threshold (with a written finding) or may waive the requirement in exceptional cases (written authorization and rationale required) [15.403-4(a)(2) and 15.403-1(c)(4)]. [5][2][7]

question: What are the exceptions to requiring certified cost or pricing data?
key_facts: adequate price competition, prices set by law or regulation, commercial products/services, waiver, modifications of commercial
answer:
The sources show these exceptions or alternatives to requiring certified cost or pricing data: 

- The offeror may request an exception in lieu of submitting certified cost or pricing data, for example by identifying law or regulation that controls the offered price, or by relying on commercial product/service information (catalog or market prices and prior commercial sales) to demonstrate price reasonableness [1].
- The exercise of an option at the price established at contract award or initial negotiation does not require submission of certified cost or pricing data [2].
- Certified cost or pricing data are not required for proposals used solely for overrun funding or interim billing price adjustments [2].
- For acquisitions funded by DoD, NASA, or Coast Guard, modifications of a commercial product are exempt from submission of certified cost or pricing data provided the total price of all such modifications under a contract action does not exceed the greater of the certified cost or pricing data threshold in 15.403-4 or 5 percent of the total contract price at award; if it exceeds that greater amount the exemption does not apply [6].
- Certain acquisitions for other than commercial products treated as commercial under 12.102(f)(1) are exempt from certified cost or pricing data requirements, except sole-source contracts greater than $25 million [6].
- The head of the contracting activity may waive the requirement in exceptional cases (written authorization and rationale required) when price can be determined fair and reasonable without certified data; such a waiver, unless it explicitly includes lower-tier subcontracts, does not relieve the contractor (or higher-tier subcontractor) from being treated as having been required to provide certified data for purposes of lower-tier subcontract thresholds [6].

The sources cited do not reproduce the full set of exceptions in FAR 15.403-1(b) or every related paragraph; they therefore may not include every possible exception listed in that FAR subsection or any detailed procedural steps for requesting exceptions or waivers beyond what is quoted above.

question: What standards must a prospective contractor meet to be determined responsible?
key_facts: adequate financial resources, able to meet delivery schedule, satisfactory performance record, integrity and ethics, etc.
answer: A prospective contractor must meet the general standards in FAR 9.104-1: (a) have adequate financial resources to perform the contract, or the ability to obtain them; (b) be able to comply with the required or proposed delivery or performance schedule, taking into consideration all existing commercial and governmental business commitments; (c) have a satisfactory performance record (a lack of relevant performance history alone does not automatically make a contractor nonresponsible except as provided in 9.104-2); (d) have a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; (e) have the necessary organization, experience, accounting and operational controls, and technical skills, or the ability to obtain them; (f) have the necessary production, construction, and technical equipment and facilities, or the ability to obtain them; and (g) be otherwise qualified and eligible to receive an award under applicable laws and regulations (see also inverted domestic corporation prohibition at 9.108). These are the standards that define a “responsible prospective contractor.”

question: What are the rules for filing a protest with the agency, and how long does an offeror have to go to GAO after an adverse agency decision?
key_facts: agency protest procedures; GAO within 10 days of knowledge of initial adverse agency action
answer:
Filing a protest with the agency: Before filing an agency protest, parties should use best efforts to resolve concerns at the contracting officer level [4]. Protests must be concise, addressed to the contracting officer (or other official designated to receive protests), and include: name/address/phone/fax of protester; solicitation or contract number; a detailed statement of legal and factual grounds and description of resulting prejudice; copies of relevant documents; request for a ruling; statement of requested relief; information establishing interested‑party status; and information establishing timeliness [4]. Protests based on apparent improprieties in a solicitation must be filed before bid opening or the closing date for receipt of proposals; all other protests must be filed no later than 10 days after the basis of protest is known or should have been known (the agency may consider untimely protests for good cause or if issues are significant to the agency) [4]. Protests filed directly with the agency are to be addressed to the contracting officer or other official designated to receive protests [4]. Agencies should provide inexpensive, informal, and expeditious resolution and may offer independent review above the contracting officer; if there is an agency appellate review, it does not extend GAO timeliness requirements (so GAO protest must be filed within 10 days of knowledge of initial adverse agency action) [4].
Time to go to GAO after an adverse agency decision: Any subsequent protest to GAO must be filed within 10 days of knowledge of the initial adverse agency action (i.e., within 10 days after the protester knows of the adverse agency decision) [4]. Additionally, when filing at GAO the protester must furnish a copy of the complete protest to the official/location designated in the solicitation or to the contracting officer so it is received no later than 1 day after the protest is filed with GAO; GAO may dismiss the protest if the copy is not furnished within 1 day [3].

question: What must a contracting officer do before exercising an option?
key_facts: written notice, determine option is most advantageous, funds available, requirement still exists
answer: Before exercising an option the contracting officer must provide written notice to the contractor within the time period specified in the contract [2]. The contracting officer must determine that funds are available; the requirement covered by the option fulfills an existing Government need; the exercise is the most advantageous method of fulfilling the Government's need (price and other factors considered); the option was synopsized in accordance with part 5 unless exempted; the contractor is not excluded in SAM; the contractor's past performance has been considered; and the contractor's performance on this contract has been acceptable [2(c)(1)–(7)]. If the contractor requests an economic price adjustment, the contracting officer must determine the effect of the adjustment on prices under the option before exercising it [2(b)]. The contracting officer must make a written determination for the contract file that the exercise is in accordance with the terms of the option, the requirements of this section, and part 6, and that the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the basic contract (for example, a specific dollar amount, a formula in the contract, a determinable fixed or maximum fee in a cost-type contract, a price subject to economic adjustment, or a price tied to prevailing labor rates) [1(f)]. The contract modification or written document notifying the contractor of the exercise must cite the option clause as authority [1(g)]. The contracting officer should base the determination after considering price and other factors and using one of the methods described (new solicitation, informal market analysis, or short time since award) and consider continuity of operations and effects on small business as appropriate [2(d)–(e)].

question: What are a contracting officer's responsibilities regarding organizational conflicts of interest?
key_facts: identify and evaluate early; avoid, neutralize, or mitigate before award
answer: Contracting officers must analyze planned acquisitions to identify and evaluate potential organizational conflicts of interest as early as possible and avoid, neutralize, or mitigate significant potential conflicts before award [1]. They should obtain advice of counsel and technical specialists when evaluating potential conflicts and developing solicitation provisions and contract clauses [1]. Before issuing a solicitation that may involve a significant potential conflict, they must recommend to the head of the contracting activity a course of action for resolving the conflict [1]. Contracting officers should seek needed information first from Government files and personnel or other readily available sources, and may use non‑Government sources such as publications and commercial services to identify and evaluate potential conflicts [2]. If a particular acquisition involves a significant potential organizational conflict, before issuing the solicitation the contracting officer shall submit for approval to the chief of the contracting office a written analysis with a recommended course of action, a draft solicitation provision, and, if appropriate, a proposed contract clause [2]. The contracting officer must include approved provisions and clauses in the solicitation or contract, consider information provided by offerors, and before award resolve the conflict consistent with the approving official’s direction [2]. The contracting officer shall avoid unnecessary delays, burdensome information requirements, and excessive documentation, and need only formally document judgment when a substantive issue concerning potential organizational conflict exists [1]. The contracting officer must award to the apparent successful offeror unless a conflict that cannot be avoided or mitigated is found; before withholding award for conflict reasons the contracting officer shall notify the contractor, provide the reasons, and allow a reasonable opportunity to respond, and if award despite a conflict is deemed in the Government’s best interest a waiver request must be submitted in accordance with 9.503 and included in the contract file [1]. They must comply with subpart 9.5 procedures before awarding to organizations owned or substantially owned or controlled by Government employees [4]. Solicitations affected by significant potential conflicts shall contain a provision that invites offerors’ attention to the subpart, states the nature of the potential conflict as seen by the contracting officer, states the nature of the proposed restraint on future contractor activities, and indicates whether terms are subject to negotiation [8]. Underlying rules require preventing conflicting roles that might bias contractor judgment and preventing unfair competitive advantage (including possession of proprietary or source selection information not available to all competitors) [6][7].
